title: The ghazals
hook: besides the Masnavi, Rumi left thousands of short love poems, many signed with Shams' name (Divan-e Shams)

segments.voice: Yesterday closed a week of guests with Marcus's ninth rule. Your line was we were made for something else. When someone was sharp, did one calm sentence do it? Day two hundred twenty, and a new week: the poems and the turning.

A songwriter finishes a song, and where her own name should go, she writes the name of the friend who changed her life. Then she does it again on the next song, and the next. For weeks we've been reading the Masnavi, Rumi's long book of stories. But that isn't the whole of him. He also poured out short poems, a whole ocean of them, sung and recited among his friends. And at the end of many, the name you'd expect to find is missing. Someone else's is there. Today's word: ghazal.
screen: `A SONG SIGNED WITH A FRIEND'S NAME.` → `NOT JUST THE MASNAVI.` → `GHAZAL.`

segments.voice: Ghazal is an old Arabic word that became a Persian form: the short love poem. It's built from a run of couplets. Every couplet ends on the same rhyme, and often the same repeated word or phrase, so the poem keeps circling back to one sound like a chorus. Each couplet can almost stand alone, a small bead on a string. And by custom, the last couplet carries the poet's signature, a pen name tucked into the lines. Rumi wrote a great many of these; tradition counts them in the thousands. They're gathered in a huge collection called the Divan-e Shams, the collected poems of Shams, along with many short quatrains. And here's the surprise. Remember Shams of Tabriz, the wandering dervish who arrived in Konya, turned Rumi's life over, and then vanished? In the signature couplet, Rumi very often names Shams instead of himself. The poems speak as if Shams were their author, or their source. Sometimes Rumi signs with a different word instead: khamush, which in Persian means silent. A poem that ends by telling itself to hush. Why sign with a friend's name? The honest answer is that we only have the poems, not his explanation. One reading: a lover losing himself in the beloved. Shams is where the song came from, so Shams gets the name. The Masnavi, tradition says, was dictated to a student and read back, a teacher's book. The ghazals are hotter and faster, often said to have come in the middle of music and turning. Same man, a different fire.
screen: `COUPLETS ON ONE RHYME.` · `THE LAST ONE CARRIES A NAME.` · `THE DIVAN OF SHAMS.` · `SIGNED SHAMS, OR SILENT.` · then, large: `SIGNED WITH HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one poem aloud. It doesn't have to be Rumi. Any poem you love, or a few lines you know by heart. If you can, say it now, quietly, slowly, letting each line land. If nothing comes, just repeat one line you remember, and listen to the sound of your own voice circling back. The ghazal was made for the ear, not the page. The bell holds the time.
Ghazal. The short Persian love poem of rhyming couplets, ending with a signature. Rumi signed many of his with Shams' name. Today's word.
Your line: signed with his name. Today, notice one good thing you do that really came from someone else, and quietly give them the credit, out loud or in your head. Day two hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Rumi's ghazals are still recited and sung in Persian, often set to music, and Mevlevi gatherings use his poems in their ceremonies.

options: Shams, the friend who set you on fire.
fork.reveal: in many ghazals Rumi names Shams of Tabriz, as if Shams were the source of the poem. in others he signs with khamush, silent.

original.note: Arabic and Persian: the short love poem of rhyming couplets.

trapdoor: what you thought: a kind of love song.
what it means: a strict form of couplets on one rhyme, ending with the poet's signature.
what a scholar hears: the signature is the takhallus; Rumi's Divan uses Shams, and often khamush, silent, in that place.

notes: Counts vary by edition: 'more than three thousand ghazals, plus about two thousand quatrains' (Foruzanfar's edition is often cited at about 3,200 ghazals and about 2,000 rubaiyat). Confirm.
Confirm that khamush is a common closing signature in Rumi's ghazals.
The ghazals' composition during sama is a traditional account, phrased as 'often said to'. Confirm.
Couplet range 'between five and fifteen' is a typical description of the form; confirm.
